title: Week 2 .NET MAUI and XAML
text:
Quick recall from last time
Last lecture was about why: every platform has its own UI paradigms, dev environment and APIs — and a cross-platform framework lets us write most of our code once instead of three times.
.NET MAUI is that framework, targeting Android and Windows for us (plus iOS/Mac Catalyst and macOS, which MAUI also supports).
This lecture is about how: what the pieces actually are and how they fit together.

title: Week 2 .NET MAUI and XAML
text:
The three pieces
C# is the programming language.
XAML describes the UI.
.NET MAUI connects the two and provides the cross-platform UI framework.
This is the part we didn’t cover last time — last week was about the problem a cross-platform framework solves. Today we start looking at the pieces MAUI actually gives us to solve it.

title: Week 2 .NET MAUI and XAML
text:
A very brief history
You know why MAUI exists. Here’s where it came from — this bit is new.
A simplified version:
Mono
→ .NET implementation for platforms other than Windows
Xamarin
→ .NET applications on mobile platforms
Xamarin.Forms
→ shared UI framework
.NET MAUI
→ Microsoft’s current cross-platform UI framework

title: Week 2 .NET MAUI and XAML
text:
What is XAML
eXtensible Application Markup Language
An XML-based language for describing the structure and properties of a user interface.
<Label
    Text="Hello, world!"
    FontSize="24" />
Declarative, not imperative
XAML describes what the UI should look like.
C# describes how the application behaves.
Not unique to XAML
The same idea appears elsewhere:

HTML describes a web page’s structure
XAML describes a MAUI page’s structure

Both are markup languages read by something else to build the actual UI.

title: Week 2 .NET MAUI and XAML
section: Two ways of thinking about the UI
text:
Two ways of thinking about the UI
We can create UI objects using C#. Broken down into its individual steps:
Label label;          // Declare a variable of type Label
label = new Label();  // Instantiate: call the constructor, create the object
label.Text = "Hello!"; // Set a property
In practice, we condense this using an object initializer:
Label label = new Label
{
    Text = "Hello!"
};
This does exactly the same thing as the three lines above — declare, instantiate, and set the properties, all in one statement.
We still have to put the label somewhere on a page, it needs to be placed somewhere alongside all the other controls. This is possible via C#.

title: Week 2 .NET MAUI and XAML
text:
The UI with XAML
Or we can describe the same UI object using XAML:
<Label Text="Hello!" />
Both ultimately create and configure a Label object.
But it might be a lot easier to read the XAML version alongside all the others.
XAML is another way of describing objects
It is not a different programming language replacing C#.
It is a language for describing the structure and properties of the UI.

resources

text:
x:Class
At the top of the XAML we see something like:
<ContentPage
    xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/dotnet/2021/maui"
    x:Class="MyMauiApp.MainPage">
x:Class tells XAML:

“This XAML belongs to the MyMauiApp.MainPage class.”

This is how the XAML and C# sides are connected.

title: Week 2 .NET MAUI and XAML
text:
InitializeComponent()
You will normally see this in the page constructor:
public MainPage()
{
    InitializeComponent();
}
This initialises the UI described in the XAML.
In simple terms

“Set up the objects described by my XAML.”







Warning


Never delete InitializeComponent() from your code, even if the compiler says there is a problem.
This is required to Initialise all the XAML components, so if you delete this none of the XAML controls will show.
If InitializeComponent() has a compiler error, this is almost always an issue in the XAML code.
Usually you need to close a tag / or a quote "

Some Visual Studio Things
When you first start a project it may have a bunch of red lines all over it - saying there are compiler errors.
This is a reason you should always compile the template program to start - clear these.
Sometimes you might have to close and reload Visual Studio.
As you go editing, maybe the XAML and C# Intellisense become out of sync so it is saying there are errors.
Always try compiling the program and if the errors remain there, they are real errors! Otherwise it is just some quirk of Visual Studio.

title: Week 2 .NET MAUI and XAML
text:
Pages, layouts and views
There are three useful concepts:
Page
A screen in the application.
Examples: ContentPage, NavigationPage
Layout
Controls how other UI elements are arranged.
Examples: VerticalStackLayout, HorizontalStackLayout,Grid
View / control
Something the user sees or interacts with.
Examples: Label, Button, Entry, Image

title: Week 2 .NET MAUI and XAML
text:
XAML nesting
XAML describes a hierarchy of objects.
<VerticalStackLayout>

    <Label Text="Name" />

    <Entry />

    <Button Text="Save" />

</VerticalStackLayout>
The VerticalStackLayout contains three child objects:

Label
Entry
Button

Think of it as an object tree
MainPage
└── VerticalStackLayout
    ├── Label
    ├── Entry
    └── Button

text:
Grid
A Grid arranges its children into rows and columns.
Think of it as dividing the available space into cells.
       Column 0    Column 1
      ┌──────────┬──────────┐
Row 0 │          │          │
      ├──────────┼──────────┤
Row 1 │          │          │
      └──────────┴──────────┘
Important
A Grid starts with one row and one column.
We define additional rows and columns when we need them.

title: Week 2 .NET MAUI and XAML
text:
Grid: defining rows
Rows are defined with RowDefinitions.
<Grid RowDefinitions="Auto,*,100">
This creates three rows:
Row 0 → Auto
Row 1 → *
Row 2 → 100
The order matters.
The first definition creates row 0, the second creates row 1, and so on.

title: Week 2 .NET MAUI and XAML
text:
Grid: defining columns
Columns are defined with ColumnDefinitions.
<Grid ColumnDefinitions="Auto,*">
This creates two columns:
Column 0 → Auto
Column 1 → *
We can define both rows and columns:
<Grid
    RowDefinitions="Auto,*"
    ColumnDefinitions="Auto,*">
2 rows and 2 columns
Row 0 has height Auto, Row 1 has height *
Column 0 has width Auto, Column 1 has width *

title: Week 2 .NET MAUI and XAML
text:
Grid cells
Rows and columns are zero-indexed.
             Column 0     Column 1
           ┌────────────┬────────────┐
Row 0      │   (0,0)    │   (0,1)    │
           ├────────────┼────────────┤
Row 1      │   (1,0)    │   (1,1)    │
           └────────────┴────────────┘
A control can specify its row and column:
<Label
    Text="Hello"
    Grid.Row="1"
    Grid.Column="0" />

title: Week 2 .NET MAUI and XAML
text:
Putting controls in a Grid
<Grid
    RowDefinitions="Auto,Auto"
    ColumnDefinitions="Auto,*">

    <Label
        Text="Name:"
        Grid.Row="0"
        Grid.Column="0" />

    <Entry
        Grid.Row="0"
        Grid.Column="1" />

    <Label
        Text="Email:"
        Grid.Row="1"
        Grid.Column="0" />

    <Entry
        Grid.Row="1"
        Grid.Column="1" />

</Grid>
The Grid is responsible for arrangement
The controls themselves do not need to know where the other controls are.

title: Week 2 .NET MAUI and XAML
text:
Grid: Auto
Auto sizes a row or column according to its content.
<Grid RowDefinitions="Auto,*">
The first row takes the space it needs.
The second row receives the remaining space.
Think:

Auto = size me to my content.

title: Week 2 .NET MAUI and XAML
text:
Grid: *
* means:

Take a share of the remaining available space.

<Grid RowDefinitions="Auto,*">
If the first row takes 50 units, the * row receives the remaining space.
Think:

*** = flexible remaining space.**

title: Week 2 .NET MAUI and XAML
text:
Grid: star sizing
We can have more than one * row or column.
<Grid ColumnDefinitions="*,*">
The available space is divided equally.
┌──────────────────┬──────────────────┐
│        *         │        *         │
└──────────────────┴──────────────────┘

title: Week 2 .NET MAUI and XAML
text:
Grid: different star sizes
Star values can have different weights.
<Grid ColumnDefinitions="*,2*">
The available space is divided into three parts:
┌──────────┬────────────────────┐
│    *     │        2*          │
└──────────┴────────────────────┘
The second column gets twice as much space as the first.

title: Week 2 .NET MAUI and XAML
text:
Grid: fixed sizes
We can specify an explicit size:
<Grid ColumnDefinitions="100,*">
The first column is 100 units wide.
The second column gets the remaining space.
Use fixed sizes carefully
A fixed size that looks good on one screen may not work well on another.
Prefer:

Auto
*
proportional star sizing

when appropriate.

title: Week 2 .NET MAUI and XAML
text:
Grid: spanning cells
A control can occupy more than one row or column.
<Label
    Text="A wide heading"
    Grid.ColumnSpan="2" />
It occupies both columns.
┌─────────────────────────────┐
│      A wide heading          │   <- ColumnSpan="2"
├───────────────┬───────────────┤
│               │               │
└───────────────┴───────────────┘
Similarly:
<Button
    Text="Large area"
    Grid.RowSpan="2" />
It occupies two rows.
┌──────────────┬────────────────┐
│              │                │
│ Large area   ├────────────────┤   <- RowSpan="2"
│              │                │
└──────────────┴────────────────┘

title: Week 2 .NET MAUI and XAML
text:
Grid: spacing
A Grid can add space between rows and columns.
<Grid
    RowSpacing="10"
    ColumnSpacing="20">
This is different from padding.
RowSpacing
Space between rows.
ColumnSpacing
Space between columns.

title: Week 2 .NET MAUI and XAML
text:
A complete Grid
<Grid
    RowDefinitions="Auto,Auto,Auto"
    ColumnDefinitions="Auto,*"
    RowSpacing="10"
    ColumnSpacing="10">

    <Label
        Text="Name:"
        Grid.Row="0"
        Grid.Column="0" />

    <Entry
        Placeholder="Enter your name"
        Grid.Row="0"
        Grid.Column="1" />

    <Label
        Text="Email:"
        Grid.Row="1"
        Grid.Column="0" />

    <Entry
        Placeholder="Enter your email"
        Grid.Row="1"
        Grid.Column="1" />

    <Button
        Text="Submit"
        Grid.Row="2"
        Grid.Column="1" />

</Grid>

title: Week 2 .NET MAUI and XAML

text:
Alignment
Controls can specify how they are aligned within the space available to them.
<Label
    Text="Hello"
    HorizontalOptions="Center"
    VerticalOptions="Center" />
Common values include:

Start
Center
End
Fill

    Start               Center               End                 Fill
┌──────────────┐    ┌──────────────┐    ┌──────────────┐    ┌──────────────┐
│[Label]       │    │   [Label]    │    │       [Label]|    │[────────────]│
│              │    │              │    │              │    │              │
└──────────────┘    └──────────────┘    └──────────────┘    └──────────────┘

title: Week 2 .NET MAUI and XAML
text:
Don’t use AndExpand
You may find older MAUI/Xamarin examples using:
CenterAndExpand
FillAndExpand
These are old patterns.
For current MAUI layouts, use:
Start
Center
End
Fill
and let the layout determine how space is allocated.

title: Week 2 .NET MAUI and XAML
text:
Margin
Margin controls the space outside an element.
<Button
    Text="Save"
    Margin="10" />
Think:
space
  ↓
┌───────────────┐
│    Button     │
└───────────────┘
The margin belongs to the element’s outside spacing.

title: Week 2 .NET MAUI and XAML
text:
Padding
Padding controls the space inside an element.
<Border Padding="20">
    <Label Text="Hello!" />
</Border>
Think:
┌─────────────────────┐
│   padding            │
│     ┌───────────┐    │
│     │  content  │    │
│     └───────────┘    │
└─────────────────────┘
Remember
Margin = outside
Padding = inside

title: Week 2 .NET MAUI and XAML
text:
WidthRequest and HeightRequest
You will often see controls with:
<Label
    Text="Hello!"
    WidthRequest="200"
    HeightRequest="50" />
WidthRequest and HeightRequest are used to request a particular size for a control.
For example:
<Button
    Text="Click me"
    WidthRequest="200"
    HeightRequest="50" />
This is asking MAUI for a button approximately:
200 × 50
in layout units.

title: Week 2 .NET MAUI and XAML
text:
What is a DIP?
The values used for layout sizes in .NET MAUI are generally measured in device-independent pixels (DIP).
For example:
<Button
    Text="Click me"
    WidthRequest="300" />
means approximately: Request a width of 300 DIP.
A DIP is not necessarily one physical screen pixel.
This helps layouts behave more consistently across devices with different pixel densities.
Why not just use pixels?
Imagine two Android devices:
Device A
300 DIP → 300 physical pixels

Device B
300 DIP → 450 physical pixels
The physical pixel density can be different, but the requested layout size can remain the same in DIP.

title: Week 2 .NET MAUI and XAML
Week 2 .NET MAUI and XAML
Week 2 .NET MAUI and XAML
text:
XAML creates objects
When we write:
<Label Text="Hello!" />

<Entry />
objects of those classes are being created.
The Label is a Label object.
The Entry is an Entry object.
They become part of the UI object tree for our MainPage.

title: Week 2 .NET MAUI and XAML
section: Working with those objects from C#
text:
Working with those objects from C#
Because these objects are part of our MainPage UI, our C# code can work with them.
We could search through the UI object tree at runtime to find a particular object.
But that would be cumbersome.
We need an easier way to refer to important controls.
Those controls are objects belonging to the MainPage class, so we need a reference to those objects

title: Week 2 .NET MAUI and XAML
text:
x:Name
x:Name gives a XAML-created object a name that we can use from code.
<Label
    x:Name="GreetingLabel"
    Text="Hello!" />
Now the code-behind can refer to it:
GreetingLabel.Text = "Hello, world!";
MainPage.xaml                                    MainPage.xaml.cs

┌───────────────────────────────┐                ┌───────────────────────────────┐
│ <Label                        │                │ GreetingLabel                 │
│   x:Name="GreetingLabel"      │ ──x:Name──────►│   .Text = "Hello, world!";    │
│   Text="Hello!" />            │                │ (the same object)             │
└───────────────────────────────┘                └───────────────────────────────┘

title: Week 2 .NET MAUI and XAML
Week 2 .NET MAUI and XAML
text:
XAML or C#?
We can configure a Label in XAML:
<Label
    Text="Hello!"
    FontSize="24" />
or in C#:
Label label = new Label
{
    Text = "Hello!",
    FontSize = 24
};
So why use XAML?
XAML is particularly good at describing:

hierarchy, layout, properties, the static structure of the UI

C# is particularly useful for:

application logic, calculations, interaction, dynamic UI

title: Week 2 .NET MAUI and XAML
Week 2 .NET MAUI and XAML
text:
Avoid hard-coded layouts
This is fragile:
<Grid
    WidthRequest="800"
    HeightRequest="600">
What happens on:

a phone?
a tablet?
a different window size?
a rotated device?

Prefer layouts that adapt
Use things like:

Auto, *, proportional sizing, HorizontalOptions, VerticalOptions, Margin, Padding

title: Week 2 .NET MAUI and XAML
text:
Think in relationships
Instead of:

“Put this control at x = 100, y = 200.”

think:

“Put this control in the second row and let it take the available space.”

Grid:
<Grid ColumnDefinitions="Auto,*">
is describing a relationship.
This is much more useful for cross-platform UI.

title: Week 2 .NET MAUI and XAML
text:
Microsoft documentation
MAUI has extensive official documentation.
Start here
.NET MAUI controls
.NET MAUI layouts
The documentation is your reference
You do not need to memorise every property.
Know how to find the documentation and understand what you are looking at.

title: Week 2 .NET MAUI and XAML
text:
Summary
.NET MAUI
A cross-platform UI framework.
XAML
A way of describing the UI and constructing/configuring objects.
C
Our programming language for application logic and code-behind.
Layouts
Control how UI objects are arranged.
Controls
The things displayed to or used by the user.
Grid
Rows + columns + flexible sizing.

title: Lab 3: Events with XAML
text:
In the previous lab you worked with XAML and created user interfaces using different layouts and controls.
In this lab we are going to put those pieces together to create a small working .NET MAUI application.
The application will be a unit conversion application.
It does not need to look particularly impressive. The important thing at this stage is getting the application working.



Compile often. After completing one section, make sure it works before moving on.
Don’t just copy and paste code. You will not learn much from doing that.
You are expected to write the code yourself.
If you are stuck, call me over for help.
If you finish the main game, move on to the stretch goals.






Open Visual Studio and create a new project.
Select:
.NET MAUI App
Give the project a sensible name, such as:
ConversionApp
Use .NET 10.0.
If .NET 10.0 is not available, you may need to update Visual Studio or install the appropriate .NET MAUI workload.

Remember: keep your project path reasonably short. Very long paths can cause problems when Visual Studio creates all of the files needed to build a MAUI application. Especially be aware of this if using OneDrive to save your files.

Once the project has been created, build and run the application.
You should see the default MAUI application running.
You have now created and run your second .NET MAUI application.




Clear out the template content so that your MainPage.xaml contains something similar (not identical) to:
<ContentPage xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/dotnet/2021/maui"
             xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2009/xaml"
             x:Class="ConversionApp.MainPage">

    <VerticalStackLayout>

    </VerticalStackLayout>

</ContentPage>
Your code-behind should initially be similar to:
public partial class MainPage : ContentPage
{
    public MainPage()
    {
        InitializeComponent();
    }
}
Your namespace may be different depending on the name of your project.



You need:

an Entry where the user can enter a number;
a Label where the answer will be displayed;
a Button which the user can press to perform the calculation.

You already learned about these controls in the previous lab, so try to create them yourself.
You will need sensible x:Name values so that the controls can be accessed from C#.
For example, you might use names such as:

QuantityEntry
lblAnswer
btnCalculate

The button also needs a Clicked event handler.
Use Visual Studio’s event-handler suggestion when adding the Clicked event rather than manually writing the method in the C# file.
Your interface should provide the user with a way to enter a quantity, press a button, and see the result.




For the first version of the application, we will convert:
Kilograms → Pounds
The formula is:
pounds = kilograms × 2.20462
For example:
10 kg → 22.0462 lb
You should now have a button click event handler in MainPage.xaml.cs.
It will look something like:
private void btnCalculate_Clicked(object sender, EventArgs e)
{
    
}
The method is an event handler.
It will be called when the user clicks the button.




The text entered into an Entry can be accessed through its Text property.
For example:
QuantityEntry.Text
Remember that Text is a string.
The conversion requires a number, so you need to convert the text into a numeric value.
For example:
double quantity = Convert.ToDouble(QuantityEntry.Text);

Important: this is deliberately a simple first version. What happens if the user leaves the box empty? What happens if they enter "hello" instead of a number?
We will come back to this later in the lab.

Calculate the number of pounds using the formula above.




We created a Label called lblAnswer.
Its Text property can be changed from C#.
For example:
lblAnswer.Text = "Hello";
Use this to display the result of your conversion.
You may need to convert your calculated number to a string using ToString().
For example:
lblAnswer.Text = result.ToString();
You can also combine text and values using string concatenation:
lblAnswer.Text = "The answer is: " + result.ToString();
Try running the application.
You should now be able to:

enter a number;
click the button;
calculate the conversion;
display the answer.



At this point, make sure your application works before continuing.
You have created a simple application where:
User input
    ↓
Entry
    ↓
Button clicked
    ↓
C# event handler
    ↓
Calculation
    ↓
Label updated
This is one of the fundamental patterns you will use throughout this module.





A conversion application would be more useful if it could perform different conversions.
Add a Picker to your page.
The user should be able to choose between at least:

Kilograms → Pounds
Pounds → Kilograms

You can use the following as a starting point:
<Picker x:Name="ConversionTypePicker"
        Title="Select Conversion">

    <Picker.Items>
        <x:String>Kilograms to Pounds</x:String>
        <x:String>Pounds to Kilograms</x:String>
    </Picker.Items>

</Picker>
You should already understand most of this XAML from the previous lab.




When the application starts, the Picker does not automatically have to select an item.
We don’t want the user to have to make a selection every time, so set the initial selected item in the MainPage constructor.
For example:
ConversionTypePicker.SelectedIndex = 0;
Remember that collection indexes start at 0.
Therefore:
0 → Kilograms to Pounds
1 → Pounds to Kilograms




Inside your button event handler, you can find out which item the user selected:
int conversion = ConversionTypePicker.SelectedIndex;
Now modify your calculation so that the application performs the appropriate conversion.
You can use either:

if / else;
or a switch.

For example, conceptually:
if conversion is 0
    kilograms → pounds

else if conversion is 1
    pounds → kilograms
You will need to find the formula for the reverse conversion yourself.
Get both conversions working.
Do not add a separate button for each conversion. The same Calculate button should perform whichever conversion the user selected.




Now extend your application.
Add at least four more conversions.
For example:

Celsius → Fahrenheit
Fahrenheit → Celsius
Kilometres → Miles
Miles → Kilometres
Pints → Litres
Litres → Pints
Celcius → Kelvin
Kelvin → Celcius
Pounds → Kilograms
Kilograms → Pounds

Useful formulas include:
Fahrenheit = (Celsius × 9 / 5) + 32

Miles = Kilometres × 0.621371
Find the other formulas yourself.
You will need to:

add the conversion to the Picker;
determine which conversion has been selected;
perform the correct calculation;
display the result.

Keep your code organised rather than creating a separate button for every conversion.

title: Lab 3: Events with XAML
text:
12. Adding a Timer
Add a timer to your application that displays the number of seconds since the application started.
The timer is independent of the conversion itself. The purpose of this exercise is to practise using an event that occurs automatically at regular intervals.

1. Create the timer
Add fields to keep track of the timer and the number of seconds:
private IDispatcherTimer _timer;
You should be able to figure out seconds!
Create the timer using the page’s Dispatcher: - Think where the creation of the timer should go - I think it should go in its own method void CreateTimer()
_timer = Dispatcher.CreateTimer();
Set the timer to tick once every second:
_timer.Interval = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1);


2. Handle the Tick event

_timer.Tick += OnTimerTick;
Now create the event handler yourself.
Each time the timer ticks:

increase _seconds by 1
update a Label in your application to show the current number of seconds

For example, your application might display:

CreateTimer should probably be called as part of the MainPage constructor, after InitializeComponents

_timer.Start();
The timer should start when your application starts.
Think about where this code should go. You already have code that runs when the page is created, so this is a good opportunity to decide where the timer setup belongs.


4. Add a Stop button
Add a Button to your application:
Stop Timer
When the button is clicked, stop the timer:
_timer.Stop();
The number of seconds should stop increasing.


5. Add a Start button

Start Timer
Use it to start the timer again.
The timer should continue counting from where it stopped.
For example:
Time running: 18 seconds

[ Stop Timer ]   [ Start Timer ]


Challenge

title: Lab 1: C# Basics
text:
This lab is an introduction to C# for students who have previously programmed in Java.
The aim is not to learn everything about C#. Instead, we will look at some of the basic syntax you will need for the rest of this module.

Note: We will not read from the console or from files in this lab. So we will not use Console.ReadLine(). The applications developed later in this module will use graphical user interfaces rather than reading input from the console. We will deal with file reading/writing later.






The lecturer will probably demonstrate this first part in the lab.
For a C# project, open Visual Studio and select:
Create a New Project
You want to select a C# Console App. Use the filters if necessary.
Give the project a suitable name.

Tip: Selecting Place solution and project in the same directory is a personal preference and is not essential.

When asked to select the framework, use .NET 10.0.
Make sure:
Do not use top-level statements
is ticked.
If .NET 10.0 is not available, use the highest version available. We will update the machines if necessary.





A new console application will contain a Program.cs file.
Write a program that displays:
Hello World!
The C# equivalent of Java’s:
System.out.println();
is:
Console.WriteLine();


Modify your program so that it displays your name as well as the "Hello World!" message.





Create two integer variables and give them values.
Add the two numbers together and display the result.
For example, if:
a = 10
b = 20
the program should display something similar to:
10 + 20 is 30
You can use Console.WriteLine() with string concatenation, just as you would use + when constructing a string in Java.


There is very little difference here. C# uses + for both numerical addition and string concatenation, just like Java.



Create variables for two numbers and display:

the two numbers
their sum
their difference
their product






Java programmers may be familiar with printf() for producing formatted output.
For example:
System.out.printf("Name: %s, Age: %d%n", name, age);
C# provides several ways of producing formatted output. One of the simplest is string interpolation.
Place a $ before the string and put variables inside { }:
Console.WriteLine($"Name: {name}, Age: {age}");
The values of the variables are inserted into the string.


Create variables for:

a student’s name
their age
their average mark

Display all three values in a single sentence using string interpolation.
For example:
Alice is 21 years old and has an average mark of 68.

Remember: String interpolation is an alternative to string concatenation. You can still use + when appropriate.





String interpolation can also be used to control how a value is displayed.
For example, a double can be displayed to two decimal places using F2:
double doubleNumber = 3.14159265359;

Console.WriteLine($"Pi rounded is : {doubleNumber:F2}");
This produces:
Pi rounded is : 3.14
The F2 means fixed-point notation with 2 decimal places.
The same formatting can be used with ToString():
Console.WriteLine(doubleNumber.ToString("F2"));
This produces:
3.14
ToString() is available on all objects in C#. It provides a string representation of the object or value.
For example:
int number = 42;

Console.WriteLine(number.ToString());
produces:
42
We can also provide a format when converting a value to a string, as with doubleNumber.ToString("F2").
You can find the other standard numeric formatting options in the Microsoft documentation:
Standard numeric format strings - Microsoft Learn


Try changing F2 to F1, F3 and F4 and observe the difference.
You can also experiment with some of the other formatting options in the Microsoft documentation.





Create a static method called PrintNumbers.
The method should accept an integer parameter and use a for loop to display the numbers from 1 up to that value.
For example:
1
2
3
4
5
Call the method from Main() using different values.


The basic syntax of a for loop is the same in Java and C#.
One difference you will notice throughout C# is that method names normally use PascalCase:
PrintNumbers()
rather than the Java convention camelCase:
printNumbers()





Create a static method called IsEven.
The method should:

accept an integer
determine whether the number is even
return true if it is even
return false otherwise

Call the method from Main() using several different numbers.


The C# equivalent of Java’s boolean is:
bool
For example:
static bool IsEven(int number)
The if statement itself is very similar to Java.





C# also provides a shorthand way of writing a simple if/else when we want to choose between two values.
The syntax is:
condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse
For example:
int number = 7;

string result = number % 2 == 0 ? "Even" : "Odd";

Console.WriteLine(result);
The condition is checked first. If it is true, the first value is used; otherwise, the second value is used.
The above is equivalent to:
if (number % 2 == 0)
{
    result = "Even";
}
else
{
    result = "Odd";
}


Create an integer variable called age.
Use the ternary conditional operator to create a string containing:

"Adult" if the age is 18 or over
"Under 18" otherwise

Display the result.




Create an array containing several integers.
First, use a for loop to add all of the numbers together.
Then repeat the exercise using a foreach loop.


There are two small syntax differences worth noting.
Java:
numbers.length
C#:
numbers.Length
Java’s enhanced for loop:
for (int number : numbers)
C#:
foreach (int number in numbers)
The rest of the loop body works in essentially the same way.



Create an array containing at least five numbers.
Calculate and display:

the total

Do this using both a for loop and a foreach loop.

text:
Part 10 - Creating a Dog
Create a class called Dog that inherits from Animal.
Java programmers will recognise inheritance immediately.
Java:
public class Dog extends Animal
C#:
public class Dog : Animal
Create a private _breed field and a public Breed property.
The Dog constructor should accept:

name
age
breed

The constructor needs to initialise the inherited name and age values.
In C#, the base class constructor is called using base():
public Dog(string name, int age, string breed) : base(name, age)
{
    // initialise breed
}

Java → C
Java uses:
super(name, age);
C# uses:
base(name, age)

Create another class called Cat that inherits from Animal.

a private _colour field
a public Colour property
a constructor accepting name, age and colour
an overridden Sound() method

Woof!

Part 15 - ToString on Object

Console.WriteLine(animal.ToString());

MainPage.xaml.cs

namespace XamlLab;

public partial class MainPage : ContentPage
{

    }
}
Your namespace may be different depending on the name you gave your project.
Do not change the namespace to XamlLab if Visual Studio created a different namespace for your project.



MainPage.xaml

MainPage.xaml
We want to remove the controls provided by the template.
Remove everything between the opening and closing ContentPage tags.

⚠️ WARNING – BE CAREFUL
Do not delete or overwrite the opening ContentPage information at the top of the file.
In particular, leave the first line(s) of the file alone.
The ContentPage declaration contains important information such as the XML namespaces and the x:Class that connects the XAML to MainPage.xaml.cs.
If you accidentally overwrite this information, the project may stop working.
Only remove the content inside the ContentPage.

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8" ?>
<ContentPage
    xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/dotnet/2021/maui"
    xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2009/xaml"
    x:Class="XamlLab.MainPage">

</ContentPage>
Your x:Class value may be different because it will use your project namespace.

For example:
<ScrollView>

            FontSize="28" />

</ScrollView>
The important structure is:
ContentPage
└── ScrollView

You will build the rest of the interface inside this layout.

Remember: ContentPage is already provided by the template. We are adding the content inside it.

What is this module about?
This module is about developing applications that can run on multiple platforms.
We will concentrate on:

Android
Windows

We will use:

C# for programming
XAML for describing the user interface
.NET MAUI as our cross-platform application framework
Visual Studio as our main development environment

The goal isn’t simply to make an application that compiles.
We want to understand how an application is structured, how the UI communicates with the code behind it, and how the same application can target different platforms.

title: Week 1 Introduction
text:
Why Cross-Platform Development?
Does everybody use an Android phone?
Does everybody use Windows?
Does everybody use PS5?
Etc. etc.
From a business point of view, it makes sense to deliver your product to as many customers as possible.
This means you will often want to develop for multiple different systems.

title: Week 1 Introduction
text:
Why Cross-Platform Development?
Websites already work across platforms.
But maybe we need more functionality than what we can build in a web browser.
We may want:

Access to device hardware
Notifications
Local storage
Camera access
Better integration with the operating system
An application that behaves like a native application

A cross-platform framework can potentially allow us to build these applications without writing a completely separate application for every platform.

title: Week 1 Introduction
text:
Cross-Platform Development
Java should work across platforms.
You compile the .java file into a .class.
That class can be used on:

Windows
Linux
Mac
etc.

This is because Java makes use of a Virtual Machine.
Even then, some issues may still arise.

title: Week 1 Introduction
text:
Cross-Platform Development
You may develop software using the same language, let’s say C++, for both Windows and Linux.
Basic command-line applications will probably work.
But what about more complicated applications?
Drawing to the screen in Windows uses a different library than drawing to the screen in Linux or Mac.
#include <windows.h>
versus something appropriate for the target platform.
The APIs may use completely different functions to achieve the same thing.
Suddenly, managing one project for multiple systems becomes much more difficult.

title: Week 1 Introduction
text:
The “In-Between”
Unless we come up with an in-between for us.
We interact with the in-between.
The in-between then deals with the target platform.
             Our Application
                    |
                    v
             Cross-Platform
                Framework
              /     |      \
             v      v       v
         Windows   Linux    Mac
For example, for Windows and Linux we could use Qt.
We write against Qt rather than directly against every operating system’s GUI APIs.

title: Week 1 Introduction
text:
A More Interesting Example
What about games?
Companies want to develop for multiple systems.
Unless you’re Nintendo.
Games are developed using the same base language, typically C++, and then targeted towards the desired system.
Drawing a triangle on an Xbox is different from drawing one on a PlayStation, which is different again on a Switch.

title: Week 1 Introduction
text:
Games
The platforms also have different APIs.

Xbox → DirectX
PlayStation → its own graphics APIs
Nintendo Switch → its own platform-specific APIs

They also have different buttons on the controllers.
We want this to be reflected on screen too.
Game designers and developers are increasingly not low-level graphics programmers.
They need something easier to use.

title: Week 1 Introduction
text:
Game Engines
Rather than writing an awful lot of if statements, #defines, or completely different projects, why not use something that abstracts that away from us?
A framework or engine can target the platform for us.
We target the framework and let it take care of many of the platform-specific details.

title: Week 1 Introduction
text:
Game Engines
You’ve probably heard of:

Unity
Unreal Engine
Godot







Unity

Developers target these engines.
The engine takes care of many of the lower-level platform-specific details.

title: Week 1 Introduction
text:
Any Problems?
Can you think of any problems that may arise with this approach?

Ports aren’t always perfect
Different platforms have different capabilities
Performance may differ
Platform-specific changes may still be necessary

For example, a game targeting Nintendo Switch may require specific changes because the hardware is different.
Star Wars Outlaws probably needed a lot of specific work to get running on Switch 2.

title: Week 1 Introduction
text:
The Same Problem With Apps
The same analogy applies to developing an app for:

Windows
Android
iOS

Even when we use a framework to help us target multiple systems, we still need to be aware of differences.
Remember GUI last year?
Remember responsive websites?
The framework helps.
It doesn’t do all the work for us.

using vs import
In Java, you bring another package into scope with import:
import java.util.List;
In C#, the equivalent keyword is using:
using System.Collections.Generic;
Same idea, different keyword: both just bring a namespace into scope so you can use its types without writing the full name every time.

title: Week 3 Event-Driven Programming
text:
Event-Driven Programming
This week we will look at how our application responds to things happening while it is running.
We will look at:

Events and event handlers
Button clicks and text input
Runtime changes to the UI
Input validation and data integrity
Properties for protecting data
Timers
Lambda and anonymous functions
Gestures

title: Week 3 Event-Driven Programming
section: From Static UI to Dynamic Application

title: Week 3 Event-Driven Programming
text:
Compile Time and Run Time
There are two useful ideas to distinguish.
Compile time is when our source code is processed before the application runs.
Run time is when the application is actually running and responding to the user.
XAML gives us a convenient way to define the initial structure of our UI before the application runs.
<Label Text="Hello" />
C# can then modify that UI while the application is running.
lblAnswer.Text = "Hello from C#";

title: Week 3 Event-Driven Programming
text:
Compile Time vs Run Time
The initial UI can be thought of as the starting point:
XAML
  ↓
Initial UI
  ↓
Application starts
Once the application is running, C# can make changes:
User interaction / application event
              ↓
          C# code runs
              ↓
        UI can change
The UI does not have to remain exactly as it was defined in XAML.

title: Week 3 Event-Driven Programming
Week 3 Event-Driven Programming
section: But What Makes the Code Run?
text:
But What Makes the Code Run?
We could write:
lblAnswer.Text = "The answer is 42";
But when should this code execute?
We don’t want it to execute immediately when the application starts.
Perhaps it should execute when the user presses a button.
This leads us to event-driven programming.

title: Week 3 Event-Driven Programming
text:
What Is Event-Driven Programming?
Event-driven programming is a programming model where the flow of the program is determined by events.
An event is something that happens while the application is running.
Examples include:

A button is clicked
The user types something
A timer reaches its interval
A finger touches the screen
The user swipes
A page finishes appearing

Instead of deciding exactly when everything happens, our application waits for events and responds to the ones we are interested in.

title: Week 3 Event-Driven Programming
section: Events Are Happening All the Time
text:
Events Are Happening All the Time
Everything the user does can potentially generate events.
For example:

Moving the mouse
Clicking or tapping
Typing on the keyboard
Pressing a button
Swiping
Pinching
Changing the device orientation

The application does not need to respond to all of these.
We subscribe to the events that we care about.

title: Week 3 Event-Driven Programming
text:
The Event-Driven Model
A typical event-driven application has:
Event source
Something that generates an event.
Examples: Button, Entry, Timer, Gesture recogniser
Event
Something that happened.
Examples: Clicked, TextChanged, Tick, Tapped
Event handler
The method that runs when the event occurs.
Event source
     ↓
Event occurs
     ↓
Event handler runs
     ↓
Application responds

title: Week 3 Event-Driven Programming
text:
Subscribing to an Event
Consider:
button.Clicked += OnButtonClicked;
The Clicked event belongs to the Button.
The += means that we are subscribing to the event.
We are saying:

When this button is clicked, call OnButtonClicked.

The method is not called when this line executes.
It is called later, when the event actually occurs.

title: Week 3 Event-Driven Programming
Week 3 Event-Driven Programming
text:
Why += and not just =
You might wonder why we write:
button.Clicked += OnButtonClicked;
\\ And Not
button.Clicked = OnButtonClicked;
The important difference is that Clicked is an event, not a normal property.
An event can have multiple methods subscribed to it.
For example:
button.Clicked += OnButtonClicked;
button.Clicked += OnAnotherButtonClicked;
When the button is clicked, both methods can be called.
Example
I mentioned earlier, moving the mouse is an event.
It should be obvious that multiple things may want to track the mouse movement.
So multiple methods may need to be subscribed to the mouse movement event.

title: Week 3 Event-Driven Programming
text:
A Button Click
In XAML we can connect a Button to an event handler.
<Button Text="Click Me"
        Clicked="OnButtonClicked" />
This is XAML syntax for connecting an event to a handler. It isn’t the same as assigning a value to a normal property.
The method is written in the code-behind:
private void OnButtonClicked(object sender, EventArgs e)
{
    lblMessage.Text = "Button clicked!";
}
When the user clicks the button:
Button clicked
      ↓
Clicked event raised
      ↓
OnButtonClicked() runs
      ↓
Label is changed

title: Week 3 Event-Driven Programming
text:
Button Events
A button has three events that can occur

Pressed: Fired immediately when a finger or mouse pointer presses down on the button.
Released: Fired when the finger or mouse button is lifted, regardless of whether it moved off the button.
Clicked: Fired only when a press is completed and released while the pointer remains on the button’s surface. If the user slides their finger away before releasing, Released fires, but Clicked does not.

Even if we are not subscribing to them, the events still happen. But we only subscribe to the ones we wish to react to.
e.g. Maybe we want to change how the button looks when Pressed happens.

title: Week 3 Event-Driven Programming
text:
Entry Events
Buttons are not the only controls that raise events.
An Entry has events that allow us to react to text input.
Two useful examples are:

TextChanged
Completed

TextChanged occurs when the text changes.
Completed occurs when the user finishes entering the text, such as pressing Enter on the keyboard.
More Events
There are many more.
The important skill is not memorising every event.
It is knowing that a control provides events and knowing how to find and handle the ones you need.
Remember, Visual Studio Intellisense will remind you in the editor of different possible events when typing in the control.

title: Week 3 Event-Driven Programming
Week 3 Event-Driven Programming
text:
Why Validate Input?
A user can enter unexpected data.
For example, suppose we want a quantity:
Quantity: [             ]
What happens if the user enters:
hello
and we try:
double quantity = Convert.ToDouble(txtQuantity.Text);
The conversion can fail and the application can crash.
We should never assume that data entered by a user is valid.

title: Week 3 Event-Driven Programming
text:
Never Trust Input
A useful rule in software development is:

Never trust data from the client.

Even if you wrote the application, the user can still enter unexpected data.
Input validation protects the application from:

Empty input
Incorrect formats
Values outside an allowed range
Unexpected characters
Data that cannot be converted to the required type

title: Week 3 Event-Driven Programming
Week 3 Event-Driven Programming
text:
IsNullOrEmpty vs IsNullOrWhiteSpace
C# provides:
string.IsNullOrEmpty(text)
This checks whether the string is null or has zero characters.
There is also:
string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(text)
This also considers a string containing only spaces to be empty for validation purposes.
For user input, IsNullOrWhiteSpace is often the more useful check.

title: Week 3 Event-Driven Programming
Week 3 Event-Driven Programming
Week 3 Event-Driven Programming
text:
Keyboard Types Are Not Validation
We can suggest an appropriate keyboard in XAML:
<Entry Keyboard="Numeric" />
This is useful because it gives the user a more appropriate keyboard.
However, it does not guarantee that the value is a valid number.
The application still needs to validate the input.
Keyboard="Numeric"
        ↓
Helps the user enter numbers

TryParse
        ↓
Actually checks whether the input is a number

title: Week 3 Event-Driven Programming
text:
Verifying String Structure
Sometimes we need to check more than whether a string is empty.
For example, suppose we expect:
ABC123
We may need to check:

The string is not empty
It has the correct length
It contains the expected characters
It follows the required structure

Validation should happen before we use the data.
The exact validation technique depends on the structure we need to verify.

title: Week 3 Event-Driven Programming
Week 3 Event-Driven Programming
text:
Why Validate in a Property?
Imagine that several different parts of our application can change Age.
If we only validate the Entry:
Entry
  ↓
Validation
  ↓
Person.Age
another part of the program could potentially bypass that validation.
A property can protect the data itself:
Any code
   ↓
Person.Age
   ↓
Property validation
   ↓
_age
This helps maintain the integrity of our application’s data.

title: Week 3 Event-Driven Programming
text:
Events and Data Integrity
These ideas work together.
For example:
User enters data
       ↓
TextChanged / Button Clicked
       ↓
Event handler runs
       ↓
Validate input
       ↓
Store valid data
       ↓
Update the UI
Event-driven programming gives us the opportunity to respond when the user provides or changes data.

title: Week 3 Event-Driven Programming
text:
Finding Available Events
Visual Studio’s IntelliSense can help us find available events.
Documentation can also be used.
For example, the .NET MAUI Entry documentation lists the events and properties available for the control.
Entry Documentation
The same approach can be used for other MAUI controls.

title: Week 3 Event-Driven Programming
text:
Timer Events
Events do not have to come directly from the user.
A timer can also generate events.
A timer allows us to run code at regular intervals.
For example:
Timer
  ↓
Wait for interval
  ↓
Tick event
  ↓
Event handler runs
  ↓
Wait for interval
  ↓
Tick event
  ↓
...
This is useful for things such as:

Games, Clocks, Counters, Periodic UI updates, Checking conditions

title: Week 3 Event-Driven Programming
Week 3 Event-Driven Programming
text:
Handling the Timer Event
We can handle the Tick event just like other events.
private void OnTimerTick(object sender, EventArgs e)
{
    lblTime.Text = DateTime.Now.ToLongTimeString();
}
The important thing to notice is that the timer is simply another event source.
DispatcherTimer
       ↓
    Tick event
       ↓
 OnTimerTick()
       ↓
 Update Label

text:
When Are Lambdas Useful?
Lambdas are particularly useful when:

The handler is very short
The handler is only needed once
The code makes sense directly beside the event subscription

For a larger event handler, a named method is often easier to read.
There is no requirement to use a lambda just because one is possible.

title: Week 3 Event-Driven Programming
text:
Gestures
Buttons and Entries are not the only way users interact with a mobile application.
Users are familiar with gestures such as:

A MAUI application can recognise these gestures using gesture recognisers.

title: Week 3 Event-Driven Programming
text:
Gesture Recognisers
.NET MAUI provides gesture recognisers that allow controls to respond to touch gestures.
Some examples are:

TapGestureRecognizer
SwipeGestureRecognizer
PanGestureRecognizer
PinchGestureRecognizer

The recogniser detects the gesture and raises an event.
Our application can then subscribe to that event.

title: Week 3 Event-Driven Programming
text:
Tap Gesture
A tap gesture can be added to a control in XAML.
For example:
<Image x:Name="img1"
       Source="Images/Mastermind.png">

    <Image.GestureRecognizers>
        <TapGestureRecognizer Tapped="OnImageTapped" />
    </Image.GestureRecognizers>

</Image>
When the image is tapped:
User taps image
      ↓
TapGestureRecognizer detects tap
      ↓
Tapped event is raised
      ↓
OnImageTapped() runs

title: Week 3 Event-Driven Programming
Week 3 Event-Driven Programming
Week 3 Event-Driven Programming
text:
Properties of a Gesture
TapGestureRecognizer has properties such as NumberOfTapsRequired and Buttons.
NumberOfTapsRequired
Pretty obvious what this does!
The event will only be raised when the user taps this number of times.

Default is 1
On some devices, taps greater than 2 are ignored

Buttons
This is particularly useful on desktop, where we can distinguish between mouse buttons.
We can respond to:

Primary — normally the left mouse button
Secondary — normally the right mouse button
Both — either button

Buttons="Primary,Secondary"

Other Gestures
The same basic idea applies to other gestures.
Tap
Detects a tap on a control.
TapGestureRecognizer
Swipe
Detects a swipe in a particular direction.
SwipeGestureRecognizer
Pan
Detects movement across the screen.
PanGestureRecognizer
Pinch
Detects a pinch gesture, commonly used for zooming.
PinchGestureRecognizer

title: Week 3 Event-Driven Programming
text:
The Same Pattern Everywhere
We have now seen many different event sources:
Button
  ↓
Clicked
  ↓
Event handler
Entry
  ↓
TextChanged
  ↓
Event handler
Timer
  ↓
Tick
  ↓
Event handler
Gesture recogniser
  ↓
Tapped / Swiped / PanUpdated
  ↓
Event handler
The details differ, but the underlying model is the same.

title: Week 3 Event-Driven Programming
text:
Event-Driven Programming in MAUI
.NET MAUI applications are largely event-driven.
The application starts and waits for things to happen.
                ┌── Button clicked
                │
                ├── Text changed
Application ────┼── Timer tick
                │
                ├── Tap gesture
                │
                └── Swipe gesture
                         ↓
                  Event handler
                         ↓
                   C# code runs
                         ↓
                    UI changes
The programmer does not decide exactly when the user will click, type, swipe or tap.
We write the code that should respond when those events occur.

title: Week 3 Event-Driven Programming
text:
Putting It All Together
Consider a simple application with:

An Entry for a quantity
A Button to calculate
A Label for the result
A timer updating the screen

The application is constantly waiting for events.
User types
    ↓
TextChanged event

User clicks Calculate
    ↓
Clicked event

Timer interval expires
    ↓
Tick event
Each event can cause a different piece of C# code to run.

title: Week 3 Event-Driven Programming
text:
The Big Picture
The important idea from this week is not memorising every event.
It is understanding the pattern:
Something happens
       ↓
An event is raised
       ↓
We subscribe to the event
       ↓
Our event handler runs
       ↓
We inspect the event
       ↓
We validate or process data
       ↓
We change the application
This is the basic model behind much of the interaction in a .NET MAUI application.

title: Week 3 Event-Driven Programming
text:
Summary

.NET MAUI applications are event-driven.
Controls and other objects can raise events.
We subscribe to events using +=, unsubscribe using -=.
Event handlers contain the code that responds to events.
sender identifies the object that raised the event.
EventArgs and specialised event argument types provide information about the event.
User input should always be validated.
Properties can help protect the integrity of application data.
Timers are another source of events.
Gesture recognisers allow applications to respond to touch gestures.
Lambda expressions allow small event handlers to be written directly where they are subscribed.
